$comment: C9 — the export gate's whitelist. A file ships because it is NAMED here,
never because nobody thought to exclude it.
This file replaces the robocopy /XD + /XF deny list that scripts/build-mcpb.ps1
used until v0.68.0. That deny list shipped .codex/config.toml — a live
Authorization bearer token — inside obsidian-mcp-router-v0.67.1.mcpb, because
the directory was created after the exclusions were written. A deny list can
only ever be as complete as the last time someone remembered to update it.
Zones are tried in declaration order; the first match wins, and the zone
decides how hard the leak scan looks at the file (see src/helpers/export-gate.mjs).
Machine-specific private roots are NOT listed here on purpose — writing
C:\VAULTS\... into a committed file in order to detect it being published
would publish it. They are passed at call time from the repo root, the home

mcpb.description: The .mcpb bundle uploaded to MCPHub. Archive layout: manifest.json at the root, everything else under server/.

okf.description: An OKF v0.1 knowledge bundle exported for sharing. Produced in memory by src/helpers/okf-bundle-exporter.mjs, so the allowlist constrains what the exporter is allowed to emit rather than what a directory happens to hold.

release.description: The source surface a GitHub release publishes. Same authored set as the bundle minus the vendored tree — a release ships source, never node_modules.

vendoredPrune.reason: npm GENERATES this directory when it installs; it is launcher shims for the machine that ran `npm ci`, not package content. On Windows it is three real files per binary (.cmd, .ps1, and an extension-less sh script); on Linux it is symlinks, which the gate refuses and the archive writer cannot represent — so leaving it in would make the bundle buildable on one platform only. Dropping it is safe because the single consumer, resolveRepomixPath() in src/markdownify/utils.mjs, is a three-tier cascade: REPOMIX_PATH, then this directory, then a PATH lookup. Tier 2 could not be relied on inside the MCPHub container in any case — no zip produced by either the old Compress-Archive build or this one preserves a unix executable bit, so an extracted sh shim is not executable. An MCPHub deployment that wants git_repo_to_markdown should set REPOMIX_PATH or put repomix on PATH.

beyondPackageFiles.reason: An MCPHub operator upgrading a deployed instance needs to read what changed between two bundles; the file is public in the repo anyway, so shipping it leaks nothing and answers the first question every upgrade raises.
The vendored zone is defined as the output of `npm ci` against this lockfile. Shipping the lockfile is what makes that provenance claim checkable by whoever receives the bundle.

scanExceptions.reason: The export gate's own test file must CONTAIN a catchable address, or the personal-email rule is tested by nothing. Every one of them is a fixture built to be found (the suite asserts each is reported, and asserts its clean twin is not). This is the narrowest possible scope — one file, one category — and it exists because a leak scanner's fixtures are leaks by construction.

Same reason as the personal-email entry above: the private-path rules are exercised by fixtures that are private paths. Scoped to this one file so a real path anywhere else in tests/ is still caught — and note that the gate ALSO caught a fixture here whose fake account name happened to begin with the real one, which is why the fixtures were renamed rather than simply excepted.

Test fixtures assign deliberately credential-shaped values (apiKey, SECRET, token) because that is what they exist to exercise — the safety code under test would have nothing to refuse otherwise. The GENERIC rule cannot tell such a fixture from a real key; it asks whether the author meant the value to be a credential, and in tests/ the answer is always 'yes, and it is fake'. Scoped to that ONE rule: every shaped format (AWS, GitHub, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Slack, npm, JWT, PEM private keys, Authorization headers) still runs over tests/, so a real credential pasted into a fixture is still caught. The personal-email and private-path categories also stay fully active here, since 'a personal address in a fixture' is one of the leaks this gate was built to stop.
scanExceptions.$note: Scoped to the repo's own exits. Exception paths are matched against BUNDLE-relative paths, and the OKF exporter strips the vault's wiki/ prefix — so without this scoping, a stranger's knowledge bundle containing a tests/ folder inherited this repo's muting. tests/ is not in the mcpb or release allowlist, but a GitHub release publishes an auto-generated source archive containing every tracked file, so tests/ IS published and create-release.mjs scans every tracked blob rather than the allowlist subset.

scanExceptions.reason: @secretlint (pulled in by repomix) IS a secret scanner: its rule presets are a catalogue of credential formats, so every AWS-shaped string in them is a pattern by definition, not a key. Scoped to the package rather than to a bundled filename because that filename carries a content hash and changes on every upgrade.

jose compares an input against the literal PKCS#8 PEM opening line in order to recognise a private-key string. That line is the parser's input format; no key material follows it in the source. (The header is described here rather than quoted: a file that spells out the patterns the scanner looks for makes the scanner fire on itself.)
zod ships its own test sources, including two example JWTs used to exercise the string validator. They are RFC 7519 sample tokens signed with a published key, not credentials for anything.
